claims.text: Demands for achievement and availability originating from work, study, social life, and individual aspirations are central drivers of high quantitative ICT use among young adults.
Perceived expectations for constant availability via mobile phones generate stress and feelings of guilt when communications are left unreturned.
High quantitative ICT use contributes to sleep disturbances through late-night computer activities and nighttime disruptions from phone notifications.
Blinded clinical psychiatric evaluation identified previously undiagnosed psychiatric disorders in 12 out of 32 participants selected for high ICT use and subjective mental symptoms.

evidence.description: Qualitative analysis showed central factors explaining high ICT use were personal dependency, and demands for achievement and availability originating from work, study, social life, and individual aspirations.
Participants reported being expected to answer phone calls and messages immediately, noting that being unable to answer resulted in overload, stress, and feelings of guilt.
Participants described dislocated sleep from sitting up late at computers and reported being woken at night by mobile phone calls, vibrating alerts, or blinking lights.
A physician blinded to the explorative interviews diagnosed 6 men and 6 women with psychiatric disorders (including depression and anxiety), none of which had been previously identified.

methodologies.name: Qualitative content analysis of semi-structured interviews
methodologies.description: Conducted semi-structured open-ended individual interviews with 32 young adults reporting high ICT use and mental symptoms, followed by stepwise conventional qualitative content analysis.
conditions: High computer use (>20h/week for women, >40h/week for men)
High mobile phone use (>11 calls/SMS per day for women, >12 for men)
Confirmed prolonged mental symptoms (stress, depressive symptoms, sleep disturbances)

limitations.text: The study was performed with a highly selected study group consisting of high-achieving academic students, limiting generalizability.
Current mental states of participants at the time of interview may have influenced their perceptions of ICT connections.
Participants sometimes spoke in general terms or about people in general rather than exclusively from personal experience.
Socio-economic factors and academic background were not controlled or explicitly accounted for in the analysis.
Prospective epidemiological studies found associations between high ICT use and mental health symptoms, but causal mechanisms remained unclear.

future_work.text: Test the proposed pathway model in longitudinal epidemiological studies combining ICT exposure levels with psychosocial demands, dependency, and lifestyle factors.
Design and evaluate tailored intervention studies targeting specific domain demands, availability pressures, and dependency factors.
